Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training

They practice in the middle of Mexico City's big urban park. With a pair of real horns, one of them plays the bull by gliding toward the fuchsia bullfighting cape. They're practicing to kill, but as the sunlight filters through the trees and the bullfighter dodges with grace, his hips to one side, his arms perfectly perpendicular, it looks incongruently beautiful.
"It's the ballet of death," José Luis Herros explains. But the movement from the bull looks too slow, too graceful, I tell him.
"That's the way bulls move," he says. When their head is down and it's ready to gore you with its horns, he explains, it comes at you slowly.
"The whole point of bullfighting is to face fear and death with the intelligence that we supposedly have," he says. "The bull has two daggers, we have this piece of cloth."
The people who gather here are real bullfighters. Mexico City has banned killing bulls so they travel outside the capital city for their sport.

As soon as I showed interest, they showed me the scars from moments that took them to the edge of death. "One bull tore my chest in half," Luis Conrado (in the sweater) told me. "But I kept fighting and I cut off an ear."
Again, I thought, the beauty of this scene was incongruous with the frank talk of death.

Moses Itauma could be one victory away from a second world title shot after a 'risky' comeback fight in January

Moses Itauma will take a "risky" comeback fight in January, says promoter Frank Warren; If Itauma wins he could then be in a position to challenge for a world title again with his conqueror Filip Hrgovic likely to make his first defence of the IBF championship in Croatia early in 2027
Moses Itauma could be one victory away from another world title shot.
Itauma, a highly regarded 21-year-old prospect, took on Filip Hrgovic for the IBF belt in August.
It was Itauma's first world championship fight. After starting very strongly, he tired, unravelled and was halted by Hrgovic in nine rounds.

Promoter Frank Warren, however, plans to bring Itauma back in a good level fight in January to set him up for another world title tilt.
"It'll be a decent fight. He's got to be in with somebody who's going to give him a test," Warren told Sky Sports.

"When you're coming off a loss any comeback fight is a risky fight. He'll be wanting to go out there with something to prove. We want to see him in with someone reasonable for the comeback fight and he wants to get back into the mix.
"He's going to have to come back and show what he's all about."

After that Itauma will be targeting a world champion. As well as promoting Itauma, Warren represents new IBF champion Hrgovic, WBC heavyweight titlist Agit Kabayel, as well as WBO champion Daniel Dubois.
"He wants to be back in the mix so he's going to be very active next year," Warren said of Itauma. "Straight in, no messing about.
"He could fight any of them. Because if he wins he'll be straight back into, I think, the top half of the rankings."

Warren added of Itauma's defeat: "Hrgovic managed to absorb the punishment. Even when [Itauma] was blowing he was still throwing shots, even when he got caught he was still trying to fight back. He did tick some other boxes as far as I was concerned."
Hrgovic is due to face his mandatory challenger Frank Sanchez next. That could be a homecoming fight for Hrgovic in Croatia.
"We're looking at putting him on in Croatia, we're working hard to make that happen, that's his dream," Warren said.
Mike Borao, Sanchez's manager, told Sky Sports: "Looking to make it happen in the first quarter of 2027.
"Everything is tracking well so far. Frank [Sanchez] is confident he'll win and is eager for his chance to become world champion.
"Hrgovic is elite and won't be an easy opponent, but I fully expect Frank to get the job done."

But the ever-pragmatic Ho will not have forgotten that. Spurs have gone from relegation contenders to European consideration in less than 18 months under the former Brann boss, but any route to the top will not be straight forward.

Speaking exclusively to Sky Sports, he said: "You're always optimistic that it can go well, but I'm also realistic that you don't just have this long-term success. It's not linear, there's going to be ups and downs, but I know if you want long-term consistency, you're going to have to have this.

"We can't just go from being a team that's been fighting at the bottom of the table to go and challenge for the [WSL] trophy and make that successful and consistent over years to come. There's a process to that but the ambition is always to be at the top of that table.
"Since coming in, I've tried to push standards, push the expectation with staff and players to give us a platform that can give us an opportunity to progress.

"The players deserve a lot of credit for that because they take the information and run with it. They play with courage, bravery, with personality which is what I asked for and their commitment and willingness is first class.

"Maybe there were times early on when I thought it was going to take a lot longer to get to where we want to be identity-wise, but the players deserve the credit because they've enabled us to maybe accelerate a little bit quicker than what I probably thought."

Part of that has come through shrewd recruitment, particularly this summer. Spurs signed Champions League winners Victoria Pelova and Alice Sombath from Arsenal and Lyon respectively, Caitlin Dijkstra also joined from Wolfsburg in just a few of the impressive incomings.
It all follows Ho's plan of bringing in different experiences from league, European and international levels to strengthen the squad and add a steel they were perhaps missing in his first year.
"We felt like we needed certain qualities in certain positions and those players that have come in have allowed us to do that," Ho said.
"They've also been in environments where they've been competing in different ways, they'll bring those experiences here which was important for us that we have a diverse environment and culture.

"You also want to make sure you get a balance also between the youth and experience of the squad. You want to get a balance of where you feel relationships can be built and where they can be long-term on the pitch.

"Alice [Sombath] was one of those in that position where she's had such wonderful experiences at Lyon of winning titles, but also internationally, she's got really good credibility at such a young age. The opportunity to bring her in was huge for us and someone we have followed for a while.

"Then people like Victoria [Pelova], who's coming off the back of a long-term injury. She was maybe low of confidence and wasn't in a place where she felt her football could go forward. The opportunity to bring her here after having those conversations was important.
"She's been part of a winning culture and a winning environment and those environments are what we want to bring to the club, which she can share and we can lean on those experiences from her.

"But since she's come in, she's been outstanding in terms of giving her the enthusiasm again to play football, but giving her the confidence and belief she can achieve what she wants in terms of own ambitions."

On October 24, Pelova will be reunited with her former Arsenal team-mates in the north London derby at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. It is the site of Spurs' only win against the Gunners in any competition, and given their rivals' own dismal start to the season, might be sensing another.
Before that though, a resurgent Chelsea - and another insight into whether this Tottenham team have what it takes to compete against the WSL's best.

"You have to show a willingness to compete in those games first," Ho reflected. "You go in with the mindset and the objective is always to win the game, but we have to look at the process behind that first and the performance has to allow you to be in that position psychologically.

"Are they going to be tough games? 100 percent, but they're the games you want to play and I want to play in as a coach, the players want to play in. The commercial interest is big in those because they're London derbies so you have to embrace them as a player.

"But they're the ones where you will really see the character and belief of the group, they're the ones where you'll really see the development and the progress of the team, but one game doesn't tell you if you're a good team or a bad team.
"It maybe gives you some answers in terms of where we need to go and the direction we need to go in, but it doesn't define you."

After a bruising defeat nearly two weeks ago, Spurs will have a point to prove in their next two games. While they might not define them as a team, it could go some way in defining where they finish come May.

Ryan Garcia is set to face Teofimo Lopez in his next fight after his emphatic victory over Conor Benn last month.
Garcia defended his WBC welterweight title with a second-round stoppage of British contender Benn in Las Vegas and is now holding talks for a fight against Lopez, Sky Sports News understands.
Fellow American Lopez also holds a world title in the same division after he sealed a majority decision win over Rolando Romero to claim the WBA belt in August.
Lopez has been ordered to defend his WBA title against Lancashire fighter Jack Catterall, but is pressing ahead with a fight against Garcia instead.
Benn is yet to confirm his next move after the second loss of his professional career against Garcia.
His long-term trainer Tony Sims has confirmed that Benn will never fight again at welterweight.
The 30-year-old announced on social media that he will spend some time away of the ring, although he continues to be linked with a trilogy fight against Chris Eubank Jr.

A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Transit, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. These flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations.

Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from crop lands and livestock farms and their interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University.

Additional low-altitude research flights with a NASA P-3 Orion aircraft are scheduled for the March to July 2027 growing season in the Midwest and California’s Central Valley with a focus on cropland.

Registration is open for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, a two-day global event on Saturday, Nov. 14 and Sunday, Nov. 15, where teams work to create solutions inspired by NASA’s most ambitious exploration goals and making use of the agency’s free and open data. The annual challenge, often called a hackathon, is an intensive, collaborative problem-solving experience where participants tackle real-world challenges created by NASA subject matter experts.

This year’s Space Apps Challenge collectively supports three major focus areas: returning humans to the Moon, preparing for missions deeper into the solar system, and expanding understanding of the universe. Participants do not have to be programmers. Students, scientists, engineers, designers, storytellers, technologists, and space enthusiasts of all ages and experience levels can contribute their skills.

"At NASA, science is for everyone, and we’re inviting the next generation to help tackle some of humanity’s most critical challenges in space through the NASA Space Apps Challenge,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Everything in NASA Science is interconnected, and this year, students from around the world can use NASA's powerful data sets to help us build the ultimate interplanetary survival guide - supporting the science that will enable astronauts to thrive on the Moon and, eventually, Mars, while also inspiring ideas that improve everyday life on Earth and in space for the benefit of all."
Supporting lunar exploration, Artemis planning

NASA continues to advance plans for a sustained human presence on the Moon through the Artemis program and Moon Base. Several of this year’s Space Apps challenges relate to analytical tools, operational considerations, and human‑system needs relevant to lunar missions. These include work related to surface operations at the Moon’s South Pole, the management of environmental constraints such as sunlight and communications windows, as well as approaches for evaluating the logistical and scientific demands of long‑duration lunar stays. Broader system‑level modeling challenges, such as those that simulate outpost operations or consider astronaut health and safety, mirror the complexity of planning for human activity on the lunar surface.
Strengthening readiness for Mars, deep space

NASA’s exploration strategy includes continued robotic exploration of the outer solar system and preparing for future human missions to Mars. Several challenges involve operational concepts for Martian surface activities, integrating data from multiple Mars missions, or reflecting the mission‑design trade‑offs required for deep‑space exploration. Others address fundamental concerns for long‑duration travel, such as monitoring physiological and behavioral health indicators, or examining how engineering and scientific choices shape mission execution in environments far from Earth.

Some of these challenges also align with NASA’s broader exploration portfolio, which includes ongoing work on future missions to destinations such as Jupiter’s moon Europa and Saturn’s moon Titan. By simulating mission‑design decisions or evaluating environmental analogs on Earth, certain challenges offer frameworks related to how NASA prepares for complex operational scenarios throughout the solar system.

NASA’s astrophysics missions contribute to understanding the structure and history of the universe. In 2026, this includes active missions like Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), which is conducting a full‑sky spectral survey, as well as the continued development and deployment of observatories designed to investigate cosmic evolution and exoplanet, which are planets outside our solar system, populations.

Challenges associated with these efforts focus on improving public access to mission data, designing tools that help visualize changes in the sky over time, and supporting broader engagement with the scientific products derived from these missions.
Broader impact across NASA’s mission landscape

Together, these challenges illustrate how NASA’s open data ecosystem enables gold standard science, by freely offering such a wide breadth of information and research. By engaging with the Space Apps event, the entire nation can interact with the kind of real‑world needs defined by the agency.

Registration is available at the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Participants can join in one of 500+ local events, join a team, and select the challenge that they are most interested in addressing during the November hackathon.

NASA is accelerating the development of three helicopters that will be deployed into the sky above Mars after a voyage aboard NASA's Space Reactor‑1 Freedom spacecraft.

Slated for launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom is the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft and is assigned the duty of dropping off the SkyFall entry capsule loaded with the trio of aerial vehicles at the Red Planet. SR-1's trajectory will deliver the SkyFall helicopters in Mars' northern hemisphere during the planet's spring season to avoid dust storms.

SkyFall is based on the success of the first aerial craft to float about the Red Planet, Ingenuity, which flew over 70 missions at Jezero Crater before it finally broke a rotor. It was designed to fly five. The SkyFall mission will consist of three identical helicopters to be deployed by an entry vehicle in the atmosphere, let loose at roughly under a mile (3,300 feet or 1,000 meters) above Mars, with each of the craft landing independently.

The SkyFall mission is to conduct investigations that address objectives relevant for science and preparing for human exploration of Mars. Anticipated flights of the vehicles will travel outside of the landing ellipse to regions of interest within a broader exploration zone.
However, there are further science-focused flight paths and regions that have yet to be determined. NASA intends for the SkyFall helicopters to go to multiple regions of scientific interest on Mars.
NASA's Mars Exploration Program, along with the SkyFall project at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), will work together to pick those "why and where" paths to navigate.

A first workshop on potential landing sites for the SkyFall mission and adjacent exploration zones of high scientific value is slated for early next year. And as always, sites and zones on Mars for the choppers means satisfying engineering constraints imposed by the project and spacecraft design.
Given the rapid development cadence of the SkyFall mission, decisions are to be fast-paced, but are geared to maximizing science value of the endeavor.

What Mars researchers are after will be a ranked list of potential landing sites that will be studied in more detail by the SkyFall project and science community, prior to a second workshop to be held in late 2027.
On the table are potential science value and notional flight trajectories of individual landing sites given the capabilities and payload of the SkyFall helicopters.
Landing site selection will occur after the back-to-back landing site workshops next year, said Matthew Golombek, SkyFall Project Scientist at JPL.
"The project has identified a design reference landing site that targets subsurface water ice deposits with glacial/periglacial terrains," Golombek told Space.com.
Given their deployment, how much real estate will the aerial vessel assault study?
Golombek said that the helicopters are capable of flying one to two kilometers every other sol, so flight traverses of 125 miles to a little over 185 miles (200-300 kilometers) are possible.
"The helicopters are designed to last 6 months, with a goal of one Earth year and each can fly every other sol so multiple flights are expected," Golombek added.

Thanks to the success of the Perseverance rover's unleashing of the Ingenuity rotorcraft, Golombek said that there are a host of lessons learned, as well as engineering additions to be made to the set of SkyFall vehicles.

"Although the helicopters are slightly larger than Ingenuity, they are being designed to operate in exactly the same way, so all of the experience with Ingenuity operations will be directly relevant," said Golombek.

The nominal payload to be toted around the Red Planet will be identical for all three helicopters, consisting of five instruments, plus engineering navigation cameras. Those instruments are to investigate the subsurface structure of Mars, the geomorphology and geology of surface terrains, as well as look at the meteorology of the atmosphere and the radiation environment.

Although there is no dedicated hardware to directly measure winds, the helicopters themselves can serve as on-the-spot wind sensors, even shifting to "Balloon Mode," whereby a helicopter will drift in the background wind.
Each low-flying helicopter is outfitted with a ground penetrating radar (GPR) instrument, one that can detect layering in the near surface, at depths unobservable by orbital radar.

Those layers could be assembled from rocky material, buried ice, or combinations of the two. Detection of near-surface ice is of interest both scientifically as well as in support of future human expeditions to Mars.
Subsurface ice not only preserves a record of past Martian climate but also serves as a "high-priority environment" that might have served as a habitat of past…or Martian life resident today.

AeroVironment of Arlington, Virginia is partnering with JPL, selected last August to co-design and co-manufacture the SkyFall helicopters. They too are building on their experience as co‑developers of NASA's Ingenuity Mars helicopter that made those 72 flights at Jezero Crater on Mars.

"Now, with SkyFall, we're taking AV's high‑volume uncrewed systems mindset into planetary exploration and showing that Mars helicopters can be built as a repeatable product line, not a one‑off delivery," said Jeff Rodrian, Head of MacCready Works, AV's advanced research and development organization.

A special "SkyFall maneuver" is to be utilized in deploying the three aerial craft. They will be released directly from the carrier spacecraft into the Martian atmosphere, where they separate, deploy, descend, and land under their own power.

"By eliminating the need for a single-use lander stage or a host rover (as Ingenuity required with Perseverance), this approach significantly reduces the technical and financial risk of getting to the Martian surface," explains an AeroVironment statement.
"Just like here on Earth, Mars helicopters can cover distance quickly and can go places that might be impossible to reach by ground," said Will Pomerantz, Head of Space Ventures at AeroVironment.
The science community may guide these helicopters to locations, Pomerantz said, where the ground penetrating radar can map out the specific spots of ice below the martian surface.
"The three SkyFall helicopters are going to show us parts of Mars we've never seen before and return mountains of data for scientists to pore over," said Pomerantz.

A new image from the European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft reveals the powerful erosive forces that have shaped and re-shaped the surface of the Red Planet over long periods of geological time.
This new Mars Express image captures Amazonis Mensa, a large, flat mountain on the Red Planet that offers planetary scientists a glimpse into the many factors that can sculpt a world's surface.

In this photograph, several features stand out to help illustrate this. Easiest to make out are the large round craters created by ancient impacts on the surface of Mars. However, many of these craters have been at least partially filled by lava flowing across the surface of the Red Planet around three billion years ago, according a statement from the European Space Agency (ESA) accompanying the image.

More interestingly, rippled structures known as yardangs can be seen to the left and right sides of the image. These ridges "form as loose sand particles are whipped up by wind and deployed a little like a cosmic sandblaster," according to ESA.

In the image, the two groups of yardangs ripple across the Martian surface in two different directions. This is because Amazonis Mensa acts as a windbreak, pushing material blown by winds in separate orientations.
For over 20 years, Mars Express has been providing scientists with an unparalleled look at the Martian surface, helping us better understand the forces that have shaped the Red Planet over eons.

Light pollution is the astronomer's biggest enemy, especially if you're gazing into deep space. And while some of the best telescopes can make a difference, there's no way to eliminate it. That's why, if you want to observe the cosmos without obstruction, you need to seek out darker skies, get a smart telescope or combine the two.

You don't have to book a flight to a dark sky reserve; just traveling away from suburbia can be enough. That's where portable telescopes come in. Set one up in a field, for example, and you'll get a vastly improved view of the cosmos. Galaxies, nebulas and other deep space objects become more detailed when they're not washed out by skyglow.
We've picked out six telescopes you can take on the road: Some, such as the DwarfLab Dwarf Mini, are small enough you could even put them in a backpack and hop on your bicycle.

All but one are smart telescopes, meaning that when you do get to your desired location, you can pick from a list of stellar sights to home in on. And while they may be portable, they're powerful with it.
So, beat light pollution and say hello to stunning views of the night sky.

Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness

- Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.

Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature, challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide new insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries.

"Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," said Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them."
Recording Brain Activity During General Anesthesia

To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia.

These procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming new memories.

The researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information.

According to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience.
The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others.

Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued.

This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness.
The Unconscious Brain Can Process Language and Predict Words
The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds.
They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus.

The results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring.
But the most intriguing discovery went a step further.

The researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue.

"The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," said Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.

This ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow.

Scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness.

"This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," said Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor.
What Does This Discovery Mean for Consciousness?
The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information.

Consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent.

This does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so.
The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges.
One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions.
Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted.
A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence
The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI).
Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next.
The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness.

Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems.
The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices.
One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak.
If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities.

"Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor.
Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain
Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered.
The experiments were conducted under one particular type of general anesthesia, so the findings cannot automatically be extended to other anesthetic methods or states of unconsciousness.
It is also unclear whether similar language processing occurs during sleep or coma, two conditions that differ significantly from medically induced unconsciousness.

Another important limitation is that the researchers focused on the hippocampus. Further studies will be needed to determine whether comparable abilities persist in other brain regions and how these areas interact when consciousness is absent.
Nevertheless, the results provide compelling evidence that unconsciousness does not necessarily mean the brain has stopped performing sophisticated information processing.
Instead, the brain may continue analyzing patterns, responding to unexpected events, and anticipating language even when a person has no conscious awareness of the surrounding world.
"This work pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious," said Sheth. "The brain is doing much more behind the scenes than we fully understand."

Arctic sea ice hits another troubling low in 2026

- Arctic sea ice is shrinking in both winter and summer, with satellite records revealing that the region's remaining ice is becoming thinner, younger, and more vulnerable to melting. Despite a recent slowdown in summer losses, scientists warn that the Arctic could experience a nearly ice-free summer before 2050.

Nearly five decades of satellite observations reveal a troubling transformation in the Arctic, where sea ice is shrinking in both summer and winter, and much of the remaining ice is becoming younger and thinner.

The Arctic Ocean is covered by a vast expanse of frozen seawater that expands and contracts with the seasons. Ice typically builds up throughout the long, dark winter, reaching its greatest extent in March before retreating during the warmer months to a September minimum. This seasonal cycle has continued for thousands of years, but satellite measurements reveal that the amount of ice covering the ocean has declined substantially at both ends of the cycle.

In 2026, Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum extent on September 12 (above), covering approximately 4.6 million square kilometers (1.78 million square miles). According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), this tied the minimums recorded in 2008, 2010, and 2025 for the 10th-lowest level since satellite monitoring began.

The maps below illustrate how Arctic sea ice has changed over time, comparing September conditions since 1990 (left), when ice coverage is typically at its lowest, with the following March (right), when it approaches its annual peak. The sequence continues through March 2026.

Satellites have continuously tracked the seasonal expansion and retreat of Arctic sea ice since late 1978, providing scientists with nearly five decades of observations. Those measurements reveal a long-term decline that accelerated during the 2000s, leading to a succession of exceptionally low ice levels.

One particularly striking pattern is that every summer from 2007 through 2026 ranks among the 20 lowest September sea ice extents in the satellite record. The smallest extent ever observed occurred in September 2012.

However, the rate of summer ice loss has not been consistent. During the past decade, September sea ice coverage has remained comparatively stable rather than continuing its earlier rapid decline. Scientists emphasize that short-term weather conditions can strongly influence how much ice disappears in any given summer.

For instance, increased cloud cover over the Arctic during recent years has reduced the amount of sunlight reaching the ice, helping to limit additional melting. NASA researchers have identified this as one factor contributing to the recent slowdown. Even with that temporary stabilization, however, September ice coverage remains far below its historical average.
The Arctic Is Losing Its Oldest, Thickest Ice
The changes extend beyond the shrinking area covered by sea ice. Scientists have also documented a major shift in the ice itself, which is becoming increasingly young and thin.

Historically, much of the Arctic contained multiyear ice, which survives at least one summer melting season. Because this ice can persist and accumulate over multiple years, it generally becomes thicker and more resilient than ice that forms during a single winter.

Satellite observations now show that multiyear ice has declined significantly. As a result, the Arctic is increasingly covered by thinner first-year ice, which forms during the cold months but is more susceptible to melting when summer returns.

The decline is also evident during winter, when Arctic sea ice normally reaches its greatest coverage. In March 2026, the annual maximum statistically tied the March 2025 maximum for the lowest winter peak in the satellite record.
Could the Arctic Become Nearly Ice-Free?

Natural climate patterns influence Arctic sea ice from year to year. One example is the Arctic Oscillation, a pattern of atmospheric circulation that affects temperatures, winds, and ice conditions across the region.

However, natural fluctuations cannot fully account for the persistent decline recorded by satellites since 1978. Rising global temperatures, together with natural climate variability, have contributed to the growing loss of Arctic sea ice.

Looking ahead, scientists project that the Arctic Ocean could become essentially free of sea ice during the summer at least once before the middle of the 21st century. Such an event would mark a profound change in a region that has maintained extensive seasonal ice cover for millennia.
How Satellites Track Arctic Ice Through Clouds

Scientists measure Arctic sea ice coverage using satellites equipped with passive microwave sensors. These instruments detect microwave energy naturally emitted by Earth's surface, allowing researchers to distinguish frozen seawater from the surrounding open ocean.

Sea ice emits more microwave energy than liquid water, producing a recognizable contrast in satellite observations. Unlike visible-light imaging, microwave measurements can penetrate cloud cover, making it possible to monitor the Arctic consistently even when storms or persistent clouds obscure the surface.

The continuous satellite record began in 1978 with NASA's Nimbus-7 spacecraft. Additional observations came from the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP), beginning in 1987, and NASA's Aqua satellite, which provided measurements between 2002 and 2011.
In 2025, researchers began incorporating observations from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's GCOM-W satellite, continuing the long-running effort to measure changes in the planet's polar ice.

The satellite maps also contain a white circular region at the North Pole known as the "pole hole." This represents an area beyond the historical coverage of the satellite sensors, where direct measurements were unavailable. When calculating total sea ice extent, scientists assume this region is covered by ice.

Eating late at night linked to up to 30% higher risk of liver disease
Late-night snacking is linked to a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease, suggesting that when you eat could be surprisingly important for liver health.

- Eating late at night could be putting your liver at risk, according to a large study led by Oregon Health & Science University. Researchers analyzed data from nearly 200,000 people and found that those who regularly ate after dinner or around bedtime had a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease, including fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.

That late-night snack might have consequences beyond extra calories. Researchers at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) have found that eating late in the evening is associated with a significantly higher risk of liver disease, suggesting that when you eat could be an important factor in protecting your liver.

The study, published in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, found that people who regularly ate after dinner or after bedtime had a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease compared with those who avoided eating late. The conditions included metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, commonly known as fatty liver disease, and cirrhosis, a serious condition involving extensive scarring of the liver.
Previous studies have connected late-night eating with obesity and cardiovascular problems. However, researchers wanted to determine whether the habit might also be associated with liver disease.

"A few studies have hinted at this idea, but this is among the first long-term analyses to explicitly draw the connection to fatty liver disease," said lead author Robert Wilechansky, M.D., a hepatologist at OHSU who specializes in liver transplantation.
Nearly 200,000 People Reveal a Troubling Pattern

To investigate the connection, researchers examined information from three major nationwide studies: the Nurses' Health Study, the Nurses' Health Study II, and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study.

Together, these datasets included nearly 200,000 participants who had provided information about their eating habits, daily routines, and other lifestyle factors. The researchers divided participants into groups according to when they typically ate, then compared those patterns with reports of fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.

The results revealed a consistent association. Participants who reported eating late at night had a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease than those who did not, raising questions about how the timing of meals might influence long-term liver health.

Fatty liver disease affects as much as 30% of the U.S. population. It develops when excess fat accumulates in the liver and can sometimes progress to inflammation, liver damage, and eventually cirrhosis. However, most people with fatty liver disease do not develop advanced liver scarring.

"It's important to remember, of the people who developed fatty liver disease, only a small fraction develop serious forms of the condition like liver cirrhosis," Wilechansky said. "Even so, the big take-away here is that confining your calorie intake to several hours before bedtime might be beneficial."

One possible explanation involves the body's circadian rhythms, the internal biological processes that help regulate sleep, metabolism, and other functions throughout the approximately 24-hour daily cycle.

The liver is particularly sensitive to these rhythms. It helps process nutrients, regulate blood sugar, and manage how the body stores and uses energy. Eating at times when the body is biologically preparing for sleep may interfere with some of these processes.

Wilechansky became interested in the connection partly because of evidence involving night shift workers. People whose work schedules conflict with the body's natural sleep and wake cycle experience higher rates of obesity and heart disease. This raised the possibility that irregular eating times could contribute to metabolic problems, including liver disease.

"We know the liver is very much in tune with the body's circadian rhythms," he said. "So we're interested in changing the timing of eating in a way that could make a difference in health without changing the composition of what people eat."
The idea is appealing because changing when meals are consumed could be easier for some people than substantially changing their diets.

Andrew McHill, Ph.D., a study co-author and associate professor specializing in sleep and circadian physiology at OHSU, said the findings strengthen existing evidence that the timing of everyday activities can have important health consequences.

"We are seeing over and over again that the timing of behaviors, whether it's sleep, eating, or exercise, really matters," said McHill. "For example, we have shown that eating during the night, when the internal biological clock is promoting sleep, reduces the ability of your body to metabolize foods as efficiently and can eventually lead to obesity, diabetes, and now poor liver health."
Previous experiments involving animals have also identified the liver as one of the organs especially vulnerable to disruptions in the normal relationship between eating and sleeping.
Could Eating Earlier Help Protect Your Liver?
Although the findings raise concerns about late-night eating, the researchers emphasize that the study cannot establish cause and effect.

The analysis was observational, meaning it identified relationships between eating habits and health outcomes without directly testing whether changing meal times prevents liver disease. It also relied on participants' self-reported information, including relatively broad descriptions of when they ate.
These limitations mean that other factors could help explain the association. More carefully controlled research is needed to determine whether eating earlier actually improves liver health.

Wilechansky is now involved in an OHSU clinical study that is recruiting participants to investigate that question. Rather than relying solely on past reports of eating habits, the team plans to monitor meal timing directly and evaluate whether shifting food consumption earlier leads to measurable improvements in people with underlying fatty liver disease.
The results could help determine whether meal timing deserves a place alongside established approaches to managing metabolic and liver health.
"Our findings add to the growing body of literature linking late-evening eating patterns to adverse metabolic and liver outcomes," the authors write.

For now, the research offers an intriguing possibility: Improving liver health may not always require changing what is on your plate. Simply giving your body more time between its last meal and bedtime could potentially make a difference.

When the end came, it must have been very painful.
In a moment of violence roughly 75,000 years ago, something sharp pierced the body of the victim, known only as Shanidar A, an adult Neanderthal estimated to be 45 years old.
The deadly injury left a gaping 15-millimeter-wide hole in Shanidar A's left shoulder blade.

We can't say for sure what made that hole, but in a new study in Scientific Reports, researchers suggest it was probably a spear, meaning this could be the earliest known example of an interpersonal spear attack in the hominin fossil record.

"The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal's body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart," says paleoanthropologist Emma Pomeroy from Cambridge University.

In their study, researchers analyzed the remains of Shanidar A, which were excavated in 2019 and 2022 from Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, one of the world's most important archaeological sites for understanding Neanderthal behavior, dating back to fossil discoveries that began in the 1950s.

The newly identified Shanidar A, whose sex remains unknown, is one of 13 Neanderthal individuals whose remains have been found in the cave, some with signs of deliberate burial, which has helped to reshape our understanding of Neanderthals, revealing evidence of specific cultural and funerary behaviors.

The most famous example of this – the symbolic "flower burial" theory, proposed in the 1970s after pollen was found in a grave – has since been challenged by some in the archaeological community, who argue animal activity may better explain the pollen.
But many agree that the repeated burials in the same spots in Shanidar Cave mean something very important about how Neanderthals laid their fallen to rest.

"The repeated use of a single circumscribed space to deposit the dead within a relatively short time-span (likely within generations…) is difficult to explain except in terms of intentional patterned behavior," the researchers write in their paper.
"The highly restricted area within which the cluster was deposited points to specific meaning being attached to this location, rather than pure practicality or sentiment."
The discovery of Shanidar A adds to the argument, but as it happens, their violent end wasn't the only remarkable thing about this ancient Neanderthal's life.
Not much of Shanidar A was recovered: only the shoulder blade, a mostly complete right hand, two left ribs plus a right-rib fragment, and some teeth.

One of those teeth showed signs of being split in half while Shanidar A was still alive, suggesting Shanidar A suffered some kind of major facial injury that broke their tooth apart, and then lived on with only a fragment of it in their mouth afterward.

"Surviving a blow that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for a period of at least a year and maybe more, would have required care and support from other Neanderthals," says Pomeroy.

"There's no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time… this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime."

While we don't know what caused the mouth injury, the researchers suggest it was most likely blunt force trauma, either from something like a fall onto a hard surface, or possibly another incident of interpersonal violence, like the hypothesized spear attack ultimately thought to have claimed Shanidar A's life.

With regard to the fatal shoulder injury, aside from the 15-millimeter hole in the scapula, the team also found tiny fractures in the bone and displaced bone fragments around the perforation, which all point to a puncture wound, most likely caused by a rounded wooden spear, the researchers think.
"Whether the traumatic lesion on the scapula resulted from something like a hunting accident or from interpersonal violence cannot be known," the researchers explain.

"Either way, the spear would have entered the individual's body on the left-hand side whilst they were facing forward. Such an injury would have penetrated all the way through the chest, including the lungs and potentially major blood vessels, likely leading to a rapid death."

While there's no surviving sign of the spear or weapon in Shanidar Cave – which isn't unusual, given how easily wood can decompose over long time periods – evidence for wooden spears dates back some 400,000 years, so it's entirely plausible that one could have caused the fatal injury.
Whatever happened, it sounds like Shanidar A's people did what they could.

"Shanidar A's shoulder injury appears to have been fatal," the researchers write, "but the apparent placement of the body in a location that subsequently became part of a tight cluster of Neanderthal individuals, who were likely intentionally deposited within living memory of each other, strongly suggests a level of care during and immediately after death."
The findings are reported in Scientific Reports.

London, United Kingdom – The British-Palestinian woman behind the Zionism is racism motion, passed by the Green Party of England and Wales earlier this month, says she has received death and rape threats since the vote.

In an interview with Al Jazeera on Thursday, Green member Lubna Speitan, an artist and activist, said she has received dozens of threatening social media messages and emails, which she has reported to the police.
“These threats were anticipated,” said Speitan, who believes they are a form of “intimidation” from pro-Israel agitators.
While “no one wants to be on the receiving end of death threats”, she said it is “necessary to confront these evils”.

The Greens passed the motion by 1,022 votes to 813 at their party conference in Brighton, but it has been criticised by virtually all other British political parties and has brought turmoil to the Greens.
Several of its left-wing MPs have criticised the move, and on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham ruled out partnering with the party, calling the motion “wrong” and “anti-Semitic”.

The motion defines Zionism, the belief that Jews have a historic claim to Palestine, as a form of racism, predicated on the dispossession and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. Palestinians made up more than 90 percent of the population in 1917, when Britain declared its support for a Jewish state in the country.

The motion supports Palestinians’ right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state in historic Palestine for Muslims and Jews. It also says that anti-Zionism should not be equated with anti-Semitism.
Fifty-six members of Speitan’s family have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.

“Zionism is defined clearly as an ethnonationalist settler-colonial project. The motion also recognises, correctly, that not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews,” she said. “It targets an ideology: Zionism.”
She added that she has been “personally smeared” by media outlets.

Recent headlines in the British press have claimed she was “friends” with an “al-Qaeda terrorist”, as she reportedly offered to testify in defence of Minh Quang Pham, a UK citizen who had planned an attack at Heathrow Airport.
“This tactic of guilt by association will not be dignified with a response,” Speitan said of the reports.
The Green Party of England and Wales told Al Jazeera that Speitan holds no party positions “other than being a member”.

“The Green Party takes all allegations of this nature seriously. Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party’s values, we have internal processes to investigate, and an investigation is under way,” it said.
Media watchdog NewsCord, which reviewed coverage of the motion, concluded that opponents of the resolution received 10 times more coverage than its supporters.

The Green Party is not the first Western political institution to classify Zionism as a form of racism. In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly passed a resolution declaring that Zionism was a racist ideology. Seventy-two countries voted in favour of the motion, while 35 opposed it and 32 abstained. The resolution was later repealed in 1991.

AsKenya marks the first anniversary of Raila Odinga's death on Thursday, the former prime minister remains a towering figure. For many, he symbolizes the struggle for multiparty democracyand constitutional reforms. For others, his political alliances raise questions about compromise, opposition politics and the direction of the movement he built.

The question is not only how Kenya remembers Odinga — but whether the principles he championed can survive. "I want his legacy to live beyond the party," 20-year-old Nairobi resident Beatrice Chebet told DW.
Chebet said Odinga wanted a Kenya grounded in peace, democracy, constitutionalism and the rule of law. She said younger generations must carry those aspirations forward.

Odinga had a lasting effect on the experiences and political journey of younger Kenyans, Chebet said. "Some of us were Gen Zs," she said. "We did not know any form of multipartyism without reading Raila.”

Odinga's influence was shaped by decades of opposition politics, detentions and campaigns for democratic change. His role in the disputed 2007 presidential election placed him at the center of one of Kenya's most consequential political crises. The postelection violence killed more than 1,100 people and displaced hundreds of thousands.

A power-sharing agreement brokered with international mediation led by Kofi Annan, the former secretary-general of the United Nations, made Odinga prime minister in a coalition government with President Mwai Kibaki. The settlement also established a reform agenda, including constitutional change. Kenya adopted a new constitution in 2010, introducing a devolved system of government.

The security and intelligence strategist Byron Adera said Odinga's impact extended beyond electoral politics. "Raila was an institution that rocked institutions, bringing about lasting and very impactful institutional reforms for the betterment of Kenya," Adera told DW. He identifies constitutional reform and efforts to bring competing political interests together as important parts of Odinga's legacy.

Reconciliation also became one of the most contested aspects of Odinga's career. His "handshakes" of reconciliation with Kibaki in 2008 and President Uhuru Kenyatta in 2018 and cooperation with President William Ruto in 2024 illustrated his willingness to pursue political agreements with former rivals.

Supporters saw dialogue as a way to reduce tensions and advance national interests; critics questioned what such arrangements meant for an independent opposition. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has strongly criticized the political rapprochement between President William Ruto and the late Raila Odinga.

In May, Gachagua called the handshake process "nonsense" and said it had eroded Kenya's democracy by weakening the opposition's ability to hold the government accountable. His position offers a contrasting view of the alliances that shaped Odinga's later political years.
The debate over Odinga's legacy is especially pressing within the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), the party he helped found and led for years.

Edwin Sifuna, a potential presidential candidate in the 2027 election, who describes Odinga as both his leader and friend, said the ODM's identity and direction had changed fundamentally. "We run the risk of losing our core support, people who believed in the ideals of ODM, because we were always the party of the people," Sifuna told DW.

Sifuna said Odinga's influence on national politics and public debate was greatly missed. His remarks point to a central challenge for ODM: whether it can preserve its identity and connection with ordinary Kenyans while navigating a changing political landscape. However, in a bid to keep the Odinga name in politics, Winnie Odinga, daughter of Raila Odinga, declared that she will run for Senator of Nairobi County in the 2027 election.

Chebet said Odinga's legacy would be measured by whether future generations continue to defend the principles associated with his political journey. Adera, meanwhile, emphasizes the lasting importance of institutional reform and building bridges.

Their perspectives highlight the tension at the heart of Odinga's legacy: a leader remembered for expanding democratic possibilities, but whose political compromises remain debatable. A year after his death, Odinga's influence is still visible in Kenya's political arguments, party divisions and public calls for democratic accountability.

The lasting test will be whether Kenya's institutions, political parties and younger generation can carry those principles forward — and whether the democratic space Odinga helped shape can endure beyond the man himself.

Researchers uncover Neanderthal remains they suggest show the oldest known evidence of a fatal blow with a wooden spear.
They also say the remains, known as Shanidar A, may show evidence of burial practices and familial care.
But an independent expert says, although the findings are "interesting", more research is needed to support the study's conclusions.
An oddly circular hole in a Neanderthal's shoulder bone may be the oldest known evidence of an ancient human fatally wounded with a wooden spear.
That's according to research published today in Scientific Reports.
The UK and Spanish team also found evidence of burial and caregiving behaviour in the species.
First author Emma Pomeroy, an archaeologist at the University of Cambridge, says it shows Neanderthals were even more complex than previously understood.
"We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature — care and violence — juxtaposed in the same individual," Dr Pomeroy said.
"We have a tendency to romanticise hunter-gatherer or pre-agriculture lifestyles as peaceful and close to the natural world … but it's not that simple."
But other experts were not convinced by the evidence outlined in the study.
Neanderthal lived with 'painful' tooth injury
The Shanidar Cave In Iraqi Kurdistan has revealed a plethora of Neanderthal remains since it was first excavated 1953.
The new study looks at recently discovered 75,000-year-old remains of a Neanderthal man in his 40s known as Shanidar A.
"Their body was placed in a very specific spot in the cave, tucked in behind a huge rock that stood between them and the cave mouth," Dr Pomeroy said.
"Over the subsequent years or decades, the remains of at least four other Neanderthal individuals were placed directly above."
Shanidar A's remains, which include a mostly complete hand, teeth and a left shoulder blade, have multiple signs of damage.
The teeth, which the team says were quite damaged, healed partially while the man was still alive.
"They must have been hit very hard in the face, which made one of their bottom front teeth split in half," Dr Pomeroy said.
"The broken edge became covered in hardened plaque showing they continued living afterwards without that part of the tooth.
"The injury would have been incredibly painful."
This, the researchers said, might indicate the man's family group provided care and support, at least in the short term.
"They likely needed some care and support from their group with drinking, communicating, eating," she said.
While Shanidar A survived the dental issues, the team suggested an unusual, smooth-edged and circular hole in his shoulder blade indicated the likely cause of his demise.
Lack of healing on the bone, and fragments found nearby suggested the injury happened about the time of death.
"It had to be something that could make a hole through a shoulder blade and all the muscle, bones and organs over the top – something like a weapon," Dr Pomeroy said.
The team hypothesised the circular hole was made with a wooden spear.
Wooden spears dating between 200,000–400,000 years old have been found in Europe.
"The diameter of the shaft near the pointed end fits well with the size of the hole in the scapula," Dr Pomeroy said.
"[But] we can never be sure because, of course, the wood has not preserved.

Sofia Samper Carro, an archaeologist at the Australian National University not involved with the discovery, said that, while some of the conclusions were "bold", the team needed more evidence to support its claims.
"I think it's a bit of a stretch with the justification they have so far,"
Dr Samper Carro agreed the circular damage to the shoulder blade was "weird" and not how bones usually break.
"Bones usually break in more kind of orthogonal … more linear fractures," she said.
However, she said, it was "very difficult" to know the cause of death, unless the weapon was also found.
"It's unusual that you get those circular shapes, but correlating that with the cause of death? I think it's a bit too much," she said.
Despite this, Dr Samper Carro said the site still had plenty to offer.
Dr Pomeroy's team is still excavating the Shanidar Cave site, examining the transition period when modern humans began to use it.
"We are investigating what Neanderthals and humans ate based on the animal bones they left behind, how they prepared plant and animal food … and a whole host of other questions," Dr Pomeroy said.
"There is so much fascinating work still to do."

Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the United States of betraying Kyiv with a “dangerous” withdrawal of support critical to its defense against Russia.

Ukraine held off on attacks for three days after President Donald Trump’s unilateral “energy ceasefire” announcement, but accused Russia of repeatedly attacking its power grid. Zelenskyy voiced mounting frustration over the Kremlin’s failure to abide by the truce and what he sees as U.S. attempts to pressure Kyiv, after gaps in intelligence sharing on Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink internet service.

Satellite internet functionality via Starshield — the military version of the SpaceX service — was being at least partially restored Thursday, according to a source in the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the topic.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday, Zelenskyy indicated his patience had already been exhausted.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelenskyy was quoted as saying.

Hours later, a fire was reported at an oil refinery in the western Ryazan region, Gov. Pavel Malkov said. The Russian Defense Ministry said Ukraine had “attempted a massive attack on the Ryazan oil refinery.”

Ukraine has been reeling from a sudden shift from Trump, who struck a diesel deal with Russia in an apparent bid to relieve pressure at the pump ahead of the midterm elections. He then demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil facilities and called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader.
Trump’s “energy ceasefire” appeared to take both warring sides by surprise. He has blamed the Ukrainian campaign for fueling a rise in energy prices, despite the impact of his own war with Iran.
The moves caused frustration and confusion in Ukraine and Europe, intensifying concerns over how much of an ally the U.S. remained in the fight against Russia.

That worry was exacerbated Wednesday when Kyiv said it was facing a slowing down of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite terminals, disrupting battlefield missions and its ability to intercept Russian drones.

Ukraine was swarmed by Russian drones Wednesday and, since early Thursday, more than 850 had filled the skies over Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. “And this comes precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted,” he said, referring to the Starlink slowdown.
Musk, a staunch ally of Trump, wrote on social media that decisions on restricting the use of Starshield were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.
Overnight, Musk said it was “time for Zelenskyy to go.”

The Defense Ministry source said Kyiv was still seeking clarification on the reasons for Wednesday’s throttling of the technology, on which Ukraine relies for battlefield communication, drone operations and air defense.

Questions are mounting about whether the U.S. has stopped or limited the sharing of critical military intelligence with Ukraine, after Zelenskyy said several ballistic strikes on Kyiv did not come with the usual advance warning from its partners.

European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

Ukraine was concerned that the chain of events amounted to an effort to pile pressure on Kyiv and backtrack on years of U.S. promises to help fend off the Russian invasion, one of the Ukrainian officials said.

Ukraine relies heavily on U.S. intelligence and the Starshield satellite network to defend itself against Russian drone and missile attacks, and also to target Russian forces with its own drones. A reduction in intelligence assistance or satellite access could seriously undermine Ukraine’s battlefield prospects just as winter sets in, according to military experts.

Ukrainian military officials were told by their U.S. counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence,” Zelenskyy said, according to the Financial Times, although it was subsequently presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch.

The withdrawal of the intelligence and simultaneous weakening of Starlink satellite internet were “dangerous” for Ukraine, he told the newspaper, adding that fighting without the U.S. would be “very difficult.”
In a separate interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy acknowledged he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s actions.
The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on Zelenskyy’s accusations and the renewed Ukrainian strikes.
Ukraine: Critical health supplies destroyed in ongoing Russian attacks

Ongoing and deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine are causing serious healthcare disruption, with more than $1.5 million-worth of medicines and supplies destroyed in four separate strikes on warehouses used by the UN there since July.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 21 warehouses have been targeted this year, out of a total of 400 incidents, almost all involving heavy weapons which is classified as firearms, tanks, missiles, bombs and mortars.

Speaking to UN News, WHO Communications Officer Sarah Tyler described what she witnessed at hospitals and warehouses that had come under attack: “When you stand in those places, you really understand what the numbers mean.

“In just three months, four warehouses used by WHO were hit and three were destroyed…The health workers I met keep caring for patients under extraordinary pressure; protecting health care means protecting them.”

The development comes amid a large wave of large-scale attacks by Russian forces across Ukraine this week. Strikes overnight into Wednesday killed at least three people in Kyiv and left hundreds of thousands without power.
This was despite the announcement by President Trump last Friday of an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.
Over the weekend, other Russian attacks included one in Zaporizhzhia that killed more than 20 people including four children.
Following the bombing, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) highlighted the “unimaginable loss” for families, insisting that the violence “must not become the new normal”.

WHO has verified more than 3,300 attacks on healthcare since the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022. A total of 247 people have been killed and more than 1,090 health workers and patients have been injured, according to data compiled by the agency.

The agency underlined that the consequences of attacks extend well beyond damage to individual buildings. “When warehouses and other humanitarian installations are hit, medicines, medical equipment, laboratory reagents and other essential supplies can be lost, disrupting the support that health facilities need to treat patients,” explained Dr Ihor Perehinets, WHO Regional Emergency and Health Security Director.
He stressed that Ukraine’s health workers face “extraordinary pressure” while continuing to deliver care.
“Protecting health services means protecting the people who provide them, as well as the medical supplies, equipment and humanitarian infrastructure on which their work depends,” Dr Perehinets added.

The agency’s support in Ukraine includes emergency response, assistance with trauma care, medical supply provision, energy resilience and developing the capacity to manage chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents.

WHO’s 2026 Ukraine appeal seeks $42 million to support 700,000 people. Continued funding is important to sustaining emergency health operations, maintaining access to essential services, replenishing medical supplies and strengthening preparedness.
WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case

The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to support Kenya’s efforts to contain Ebola after a second person tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus, the UN agency’s representative in the country said on Thursday.
The patient, a 39-year-old man, is a relative of Kenya’s first case – related to the ongoing deadly outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – who died in hospital on 5 October.
He was among contacts who were placed in quarantine and developed symptoms on 13 October.

“I congratulate the Government for taking this important step to ensure that contacts are listed and quarantined,” WHO Representative Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo told UN News in Nairobi, a day after the Ministry of Health confirmed the new case.

“But to defeat this disease, it's not about the Government, it is not about partners It is about everybody,” she insisted. “We all have a role to play and if each one of us plays our part, then we should be able to contain the disease and stop community spread.”
Kenya’s first Ebola patient and fatality was a local man who had been living in the DRC, where the record outbreak continues to spread in the east.
He arrived in Nairobi via Uganda on 3 October and died in hospital two days later.
Dr. Kimambo commended health authorities who “cast the net very wide” to identify people who had come into contact with him – whether in the air or on the ground.
The more than 40 people included airline passengers and crew, airplane cleaners, airport workers, baggage handlers and immigration officials, as well as health personnel and family members.

Most are in quarantine, while a few low-risk contacts have self-quarantined and are being monitored. Meanwhile, every effort is being made to reach six passengers who have been difficult to locate because they have foreign phone numbers.

Even before the first case , WHO and the Kenyan Government were stepping up Ebola preparedness after the outbreak was declared in the DRC in May. Neighbouring Uganda also confronted the disease, with any outbreak officially ruled out in late August.

Teams are working across all areas, including surveillance and contact tracing. WHO has also brought in a senior incident manager who participated in the Ebola response in Uganda, as well as other experts.

“We are building on the work that we started during the preparedness phase, so case management and IPC (infection prevention and control) are critical at this time in the quarantine centres,” Dr. Kimambo said.

WHO also continues to provide assistance to Kenya in various other ways. The UN agency has donated some $70,000 worth of supplies, including IPC and laboratory items, since the first Ebola case was identified.
Additionally, more than 4,000 health workers have been trained, including for screenings at ports of entry.

While Dr. Kimambo said there still is no need to impose travel restrictions or close national borders, she underlined the importance of appropriate screening to identify travellers who may pose a health risk.
Preventing Ebola begins with understanding how the disease is transmitted, she said, which is through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person.
She reiterated the advice to practice regular handwashing, use hand sanitizer and avoid shaking hands.

As Ebola symptoms include fever, vomiting and diarrhoea – which mimic symptoms of malaria and other diseases – she stressed the need to seek medical care quickly. In the interim, Kenyans are urged to keep calm and stay safe.

“I think one is not to over panic and be very fearful because we do not have community spread,” she said. “But two, let us be responsible. Whoever is sick, let’s make sure we go to a health facility and get care. And also, let us ensure that we take IPC measures.”

BELLEVUE, Wash., Oct. 15, 2026 — Agile Space Industries, a leading provider of in-space chemical propulsion solutions, has expanded into the Seattle metropolitan area with the opening of a new office in Bellevue, Washington. The expansion builds on Agile’s continued growth, extending its engineering capabilities and strengthening its presence in one of the nation’s most established aerospace and technology markets.

Located at Sunset North in Bellevue, the new 5,470-square-foot office will initially accommodate 7 employees, with the capacity to grow to approximately 30 as Agile expands its regional operations. Agile Chief Technology Officer Jake Mills will be based at the Bellevue office, reinforcing the company’s commitment to establishing a strong engineering and leadership presence in the region.

“Seattle has a remarkable concentration of aerospace talent, innovative companies and organizations advancing the space industry,” said Jake Mills, chief technology officer at Agile Space Industries. “Establishing a presence here allows us to tap into that expertise, strengthen industry relationships and build on the capabilities we’re developing across Agile to support our customers and their missions.”

The Bellevue office will focus on engineering and program management, supporting the development and delivery of advanced propulsion systems for government and commercial space missions. As the team grows, Agile expects to broaden its technical expertise and support an expanding range of propulsion programs.

Beyond its engineering talent, the Seattle region offers an established network of aerospace companies, industry partners and investors. Agile’s presence in this ecosystem creates opportunities to strengthen customer relationships, develop new partnerships and engage with the broader business and investment community as the company pursues its long-term growth objectives.

The expansion also creates opportunities for experienced aerospace professionals looking to work on complex propulsion challenges in a collaborative, hands-on engineering environment. Agile’s teams contribute to programs spanning early development through qualified flight hardware, with the opportunity to help shape technologies supporting the next generation of space missions.

The Bellevue office joins Agile’s headquarters in Durango, Colorado, and operations in Pennsylvania and Oklahoma. Together, these locations support Agile’s growing capabilities in propulsion design, manufacturing and testing, positioning the company to serve an expanding range of commercial and government space customers.

Agile Space Industries develops advanced chemical propulsion solutions that enable spacecraft to move, maneuver, and operate in space. From early concepts to qualified flight hardware, Agile brings together propulsion expertise, additive manufacturing, and in-house testing to rapidly solve complex challenges and accelerate development. Agile partners with leading aerospace companies and the U.S. Government on spacecraft and launch vehicle programs. Learn more at agilespaceindustries.com.
